elements.text: Just finished the concurrent download load balancer. As we currently run a configured number of channels and distribute downloads to each in a configured set size, it is easy for channels to become starved for work and then just idle until others are done. This results in all but one channel idling toward completion. I resolved this in prototyping by selecting the slowest channel with work for termination, splitting its work into two sets, and notifying channels of new work. Dropping the channel has a small cost, but the channel cannot be retained as that would results in a significant level of duplicate block downloads, or very inefficient single block requests. Since channels are recovered very quickly (earlier work from last year) the cost is trivial.

announced hot backup, we have something very close. The node can be snapshotted while running, but not externally - it must be invoked on the running command line. elements.text: The snapshot flushes table bodies, just to ensure they are written to disk, and then copies headers from memory into a new index directory. So the snapshot constitutes the full set of headers and the corrupted bodies. But as the bodies are append only, they are perfectly valid given the uncorrupted headers. Furthermore the logical body size is retained by the header, so during restore the bodies are truncated. As a result, as long as a live snapshot has been taken an external full backup can be made by copying the snapshot directory and the body directory. This can be done safely against the '/secondary' directory (as opposed to '/primary' since the former is always created by a file system directory rename from primary - ensuring that its files are a consistent and complete set.

elements.text: The key design principle is based on Amir's append only design, however that suffered from hash table headers being co-located within the body files. The headers are random write access and cannot be recovered in case of a fault. Also memory maps must be flushed before they can be relied upon upon shutdown or for hot copy. This of course also required that indexation spanning multiple files was logically atomic. So to resolve these issues we split the headers and bodies, enforced true append only on the bodies, created a transactional commit system using a mutex-based transactor (only locked during backup, so not a performance consideration), created a method to pause channel reads (thereby suspending store writes) without dropping channels, and implemented flush to disk of all files after obtaining the exclusive transactor and before taking index snapshots.

elements.text: Another interesting aspect of the memory map store that I forgot to mention is that, when a map for a given file needs to be made larger the operating system can remap it. In other words, invalidate all outstanding pointers into the map. This was another aspect that hadn't been dealt in the original implementation. This requires, on a per file basis, that each read/write pointer obtained from the store is an object that encapsulates a remap mutex. When the map allocation is exceeded for the given file, the store blocks until all shared locks are released and then holds exclusive access during the remap. This requires that all pointers are very short lived and cannot be passed into code that could be waiting on another pointer (deadlock). This was something that I implemented in the prototype, but it wasn't sufficiently safe. So in the current store reads and writes encapsulated within low level store primitives which manage memory access, passing higher level result sets back to the query implementations, and these providing the custom query interface that the store exposes publicly.
